# The Willpower Method

> "For I don't practice what I desire to do; but what I hate, that I do."
>
> — Romans 7:15

Everybody knows that stopping is hard. The forums say so. The apps say so. The men who have tried say so, and add that it will be misery for the rest of your life. Nearly every book on the subject opens by warning you what a brutal road lies ahead.

The truth is that it's absurdly easy.

I know how that sounds. Bear with me. If I told you to run a marathon in under three hours, that would be hard. You'd need years of training, and you might not have the legs for it however hard you trained. But stopping the habit doesn't ask you to *do* anything. You only have to not do something. Nobody is holding you down and making you. Your body doesn't need it the way it needs bread and water. So if you want to stop, where exactly is the difficulty?

There isn't one. Men create the difficulty themselves, by using the Willpower Method. I mean any way of quitting that leaves you feeling you've sacrificed something. It is the same method whether the thing is porn, the hand or a woman you keep going back to. A man blocks the sites and unblocks them. He deletes her number and finds it again. We'll follow the habit here, because it shows the pattern most plainly. Let's look at how it goes.

It usually takes years to realize you're hooked, because of one stubborn illusion: we assume men do this because they enjoy it. So on the nights we plainly don't enjoy it, we conclude we could stop any time. "I don't even like it that much. I could drop it tomorrow." That's the confidence trap. Somehow tomorrow is never the day you want to.

## The first attempts {-}

After a few failed attempts, a man generally falls back on hope. One morning, he tells himself, he'll just wake up and not want it anymore. The hope gets fed by stories. "My cousin just stopped. Got married and never thought about it again." Don't be fooled. Look into those stories and they're never that simple. Either the man had been working up to it for a year and the wedding was the last push, or he'd had a fright. No man has ever drifted out of this trap by accident. **It won't happen unless you make it happen.**

## Why willpower is so hard {-}

Let's slow down and watch the Willpower Method work.

For most of our lives we keep our heads in the sand: "I'll deal with it later." Every so often something jolts us into an attempt. So we sit down and add it up. On one side go the shame, the tiredness, the wasted hours, the distance from God and the look we can't give our partner. And on the other side? What, exactly? Any honest tally comes out the same, and it has since we were fifteen: **Stop. You're being a fool.**

So he knows he'd be better off without it. That was never in doubt. What trips him is something else: he believes he's making a sacrifice. He can't say what it is he's sacrificing. He only has a feeling that in the good times and the bad times alike, the habit *helps*. It's an illusion, but it's a strong one.

On top of that sit the lies he's soaked up from the world. On top of those sits the heaviest lie of all, which is how terrible it is to quit. He's heard about the man ninety days clean who still thinks about it every hour. He's heard about the man who says it has been a nightly war for fifty years. He's read about the man who set himself five years, reached day 280, and lost it in one lonely evening. He may know one or two men who are obviously being eaten by this and still can't stop. Most likely he's lived some of those stories himself.

So he doesn't start out thinking, "Wonderful! Have you heard? I don't have to do this anymore!" He starts in dread, like a man looking up at a cliff he has to climb. He texts his accountability partner: "Pray for me. This month is going to be rough." Most attempts are beaten before they begin.

A psychiatrist who treats porn addiction gives the reason the fighting fails: "willpower is a diminishing resource so the more you use it the less you have to resist".

Suppose he gets through the first few days. He feels a bit brighter. There's a little more spring in the mornings. And the reasons that made him stop are already fading. It's like passing a crash on the highway. You ease off for ten miles, shaken, and by the time you're running late again your foot is back on the floor.

Meanwhile the Little Monster hasn't been fed. There's no pain in it. If a head cold made you feel like that, you wouldn't even mention it. But he knows what he wants. So the Little Monster wakes the Big Monster, and now watch something remarkable. The very man who three days ago was listing every reason to stop starts hunting, just as earnestly, for a reason to start:

- "Life's short. There are worse sins."
- "I chose the wrong week."
- "I can't think straight. I'm snapping at everyone. I can't do my job like this."
- "It isn't even mentioned in the Bible."
- "Better this than going back to porn."
- "I'll just see how she's doing. It's only a message."
- "God made men this way. He can't expect the impossible."

This is the point where he gives in.

What follows is the strangest minute of all. He feels real relief, because the Little Monster has been fed and has stopped nagging. In the same minute there's the flatness, and the old question: *why did I do that?* He draws the obvious conclusion that he's weak and has no willpower.

It wasn't only weakness. He changed his mind. Look at what he believed at that moment. He was suffering. The habit would end the suffering. There was something in it for him after all. Given all that, going back was a perfectly logical decision. His will was tired, but that wasn't the whole story. He was also acting on false information, and that part this book can fix.

"What's the point of a clean conscience if I'm miserable?" It's a fair question, and the answer is that you won't be. A life without the habit isn't gray and twitchy. Notice where his misery comes from. It doesn't come from the Little Monster, who is tiny. It comes from the tug-of-war. He starts by believing he's given something up, so he feels deprived, and feeling deprived is itself a strain. In a strain, the old voice says "go on", and now he can't. So he feels more deprived still.

## The counter {-}

One feature of the Willpower Method makes it worse than everything else, and in our day it has been built into the phone.

If you take a driving test, you know the moment you've passed, because the examiner tells you. On the Willpower Method nobody tells you. The plan is: "If I can just go long enough without it, the wanting will stop." How long is long enough? Nobody can tell you. So you count.

The big online movement has made a ritual of this. There are day counters and badges. There is a ninety-day target that its own site describes as "difficult for most, yet achievable." When a man falls, he performs the routine the site calls a reset: "Resetting means restarting their challenge beginning with day one and starting again."

Think about what a counter actually measures. It measures the distance between you and the last time you did it. So every morning it points you back at the habit, the very thing you're trying to leave behind. A man with a streak thinks about porn and masturbation more than a man without one. He has to. He's keeping score.

Scroll down under any video on this subject and you'll find the same routine in the comments, posted again and again by different men: "Day 1 of quitting." Each man means it with his whole heart. And each has asked a crowd of strangers to remind him, every time they press a button, of the thing he's trying to forget.

And who counts days? A man scratching lines on a cell wall counts days. A free man has no idea how many days it's been since he was released. He's got better things to do. Ask a man who used to bite his nails how many days it has been. He couldn't tell you. Each number on that counter says "day forty of doing without", and a man who's doing without has decided in advance that he's losing something.

Then there's the reset. One slip on day sixty-one and the screen says zero. All of it gone! So what does the man at zero do? More often than not he thinks, "Well, it's ruined now," and makes a weekend of it before starting the count again on Monday. The counter turned one bad night into three. A man who had quit for good and stumbled would pick himself up the same hour. The man with a counter has to start again from the bottom of the hill.

So the man on the Willpower Method waits. And while he waits, the questions come:

- "How long is this going to last?"
- "Will I ever enjoy a quiet evening again?"
- "Will I ever sleep properly?"
- "What will I do the next time everything goes wrong?"

He's waiting for things to get better, and while he mopes, the thing he's given up grows more precious by the day. The miserable men on those forums aren't suffering from withdrawal. What hurts them is doubt.

## The honest man in Romans 7 {-}

If you want the Willpower Method described by someone who wasn't selling an app, read Paul. In Romans 7 he writes:

"For the good which I desire, I don't do; but the evil which I don't desire, that I practice."

That is as honest a sentence as any man has written about himself. And Paul was no weakling. He was beaten, shipwrecked and pelted with stones, and he kept going. If grit were the cure, he had more of it than you or I ever will. Yet when his own will went up against his own flesh, he lost, and he said so.

There are two wills in you. One of them wants to be free and the other wants one more night. The Willpower Method is the plan of setting the first to overpower the second, every day, for good. But it's all one man. You're arm-wrestling yourself, and whichever arm wins, you're the one who's tired. One commenter wrote a line that thousands of men endorsed: "Every time I think I've escaped this sin, it comes back at me like a bite of a snake."

These men aren't lazy and they aren't faithless. They tried as hard as anyone could, and trying harder was the one thing that couldn't work.

Now look at how Paul ends the chapter. "What a wretched man I am! Who will deliver me out of the body of this death? I thank God through Jesus Christ, our Lord!"

His question isn't "*how* shall I try harder?" It's "*who* will deliver me?" The answer is a person and a gift, and it comes with a shout of thanks. He never mentions a technique.

Notice who described this first. Paul wrote those sentences nearly two thousand years ago, long before anyone made an app to count days.

If you're not a believer, stay with me, because part of this holds without the theology. The war between two wills doesn't end when one of them finally wins. **IT ENDS WHEN ONE OF THEM IS GONE.** The will that wants "one more night" lives entirely on the belief that the night has something to offer. Take away the belief and there's no second will left to fight. That's what this book is doing, a chapter at a time. For a believer, that is the work Paul gave thanks for. It is done by the one who delivers, and this book is only clearing the ground for it.

## Meanwhile, on day forty {-}

Back to our man on his streak, because something really is happening to him, though he can't feel it. If he lasts a few weeks, the Little Monster starves. The bodily itch is so slight that he never notices it die.

Around then he feels he's cracked it. So he allows himself one, to prove the point, or to celebrate, or just to see. He does it, and it's a let-down, as it always was. But the Little Monster has had a meal, and next day there's a small voice asking for another. He had been out, and he's walked back in.

He doesn't go straight back to nightly. He's careful and leaves it a week or two. Then he reasons, "I had one and didn't get hooked, so one more is safe." That's the same reasoning he used at thirteen, and it works the same way now.

Some men do succeed on willpower. I don't want to take anything away from them. But listen to how they tell it. It was long and it was bitter, because the lie was still in their heads the whole time. The Little Monster had been dead for months and they were still moping. At last it dawned on them that they weren't going to give in, the moping stopped, and they found that life went on perfectly well.

Many more fail than succeed that way. And some who succeed stay fragile for the rest of their lives, because a corner of them still believes the habit had something to give. That's why a man can be ten years clear and fall in one bad week. One commenter put all of it into a single line: "I thought I had Kicked the habit but the habit came back."

## Enjoyment never came into it {-}

Everything hangs on this, so it is worth saying plainly. Enjoyment has nothing to do with this, and it never did. If men did it for enjoyment, they wouldn't do it when they're sick, or exhausted, or an hour after they'd promised God. We only assume we enjoy it because the alternative is too insulting to consider. The alternative is that we've been doing something for twenty years that gives us nothing.

That's also why most of it happens half-asleep, on autopilot, in the dark. Suppose you could watch a man at this habit. You'd see he's only content while he isn't thinking about what he's doing. The moment he thinks about it, he's uneasy.

The Willpower Method gets self-control wrong. It thinks self-control means holding a door shut for the rest of your life against something heavy leaning on the other side. That isn't self-control. It's a siege, and sooner or later the man inside gets tired. A soldier who spends every watch wrestling the bottle isn't fit for duty either.

He is only dry.

Real self-control looks different. There's nothing leaning on the door. The man opens it and shuts it as he pleases, and half the time he forgets it's there.

The old Christians who say a man must keep watch his whole life are right. Peter, one of the twelve men closest to Jesus, said, "Be sober and self-controlled. Be watchful." But a watchman isn't a man wrestling a thing on the other side of the door every night. He's a man who knows what's out there and isn't afraid of it.

The habit feeds the Little Monster. The lies are the Big Monster. Starve the first, clear out the second, and you will have **NEITHER THE NEED NOR THE WISH** to go back to any of it.
